memory_update.text: Restaurants theme should be mapped around infrastructure nodes: broadline distribution, specialty distribution, ethnic distribution, cash-and-carry procurement, route-density logistics, cold-chain, franchise supply-chain orchestration, labor/service capacity, B2B beverage supply, sanitation/QA, packaging, and restaurant software.

Highest preliminary bottleneck scores belong to route-density logistics, specialty foodservice distribution, broadline distribution, franchise supply-chain orchestration, and independent restaurant procurement.

Low-attention bottleneck value may hide in specialty and ethnic distributors, food-safety certification gates, sanitation/HI&I suppliers, B2B beverage/private-label suppliers, cold-chain/refrigeration, packaging compliance, and restaurant software/data tools.
Distributor consolidation and any change in cash-and-carry channel structure should be tracked as a catalyst for independent restaurant procurement costs and supplier bargaining power.

Distributor earnings metrics to track: independent restaurant case growth, customer retention, gross-margin durability, delivery productivity, EBITDA per case, digital ordering adoption, acquisition integration, and fuel/labor efficiency.

Franchise growth catalysts should be tested through franchisee unit economics, commodity costs, delivery-driver availability, service times, distribution partnerships, and centralized supply-chain support.

Coffee and beverage growth can catalyze B2B suppliers, proprietary beverage inputs, equipment, loyalty/data vendors, and drive-thru infrastructure, but many emerging concepts remain unprofitable and execution-sensitive.
Need direct filing evidence for non-distributor candidates' restaurant or foodservice revenue exposure, especially sanitation, specialty chemicals, packaging, equipment, QA, and software names.

Need broader company universe beyond cached distributor-heavy Layer 1: packaging, refrigeration, pest control, food-safety audits, coffee/B2B beverage, labor scheduling, POS/loyalty, equipment, grease/used-oil management, and protein suppliers.
Need market-cap, liquidity, analyst-coverage, customer concentration, and filing verification to separate reference leaders from true underfollowed candidates.

CHEF is the highest-priority underfollowed relationship in the current Restaurants chunk because it maps directly to specialty restaurant procurement, premium SKU access, route density, and fragmented-distribution roll-up economics.

SYY, USFD, and PFGC should be retained as reference leaders for route-density logistics, procurement scale, independent restaurant case growth, and national-chain distribution benchmarks, not as underfollowed discovery names.

HFFG is a speculative shadow candidate for ethnic and Asian foodservice distribution; it requires governance, liquidity, gross-margin, customer-retention, and distribution-center utilization checks before any upgrade.
ACNT has insufficient direct evidence tying specialty chemicals or HI&I revenue to restaurants or foodservice; require filing-level customer/channel proof before retaining it in Layer 3.

REBN is better treated as a distribution-dependency read-through than a supplier chokepoint; verify whether the Sysco partnership materially changes unit economics, product consistency, or franchise rollout capacity.

The current chunk remains overconcentrated in foodservice distribution. Next candidate expansion should target packaging/disposables, food-safety audits and traceability, sanitation chemicals, pest control, grease/used-oil management, refrigeration equipment, cold-chain logistics, B2B coffee/beverage inputs, and restaurant software.

Distributor consolidation and possible Restaurant Depot-related procurement changes are important catalysts, but current evidence comes from external analysis rather than primary transaction filings; verify transaction status and regulatory documents before using as a fact.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Layer 2A maps Restaurants as an operating system rather than only consumer-facing chains. The highest-chokepoint nodes appear to be foodservice distribution, specialty/ethnic distribution, franchise supply-chain orchestration, route-density logistics, labor/service capacity, food input volatility, beverage/coffee B2B supply, restaurant technology/data rails, sanitation/food-safety compliance, and off-premise packaging/cold-chain infrastructure. High-attention restaurant brands should not dominate the funnel; lower-attention value may hide in distributors, route-density networks, QA/compliance vendors, B2B beverage suppliers, specialty procurement channels, and software/data tools that improve franchisee economics or independent restaurant survival.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurant revenue depends on traffic, ticket size, menu pricing, value perception, and consumer income sensitivity. This is the visible demand layer, but it is often less bottlenecked than the infrastructure layers that determine operator margins.

Independent restaurants usually lack the purchasing scale of large chains and are more exposed to distributor consolidation, cash-and-carry availability, commodity inflation, and limited supplier alternatives.

Broadline distributors aggregate procurement, warehousing, delivery, ordering, food-safety resources, and multi-SKU fulfillment. Scale and route density can create structural advantages, but mega-cap leaders should be treated as reference nodes rather than the only investable map.

Specialty distributors serve menu-driven independent restaurants, fine dining, hotels, caterers, bakeries, cruise lines, casinos, and other niche customers. Bottleneck value may hide in SKU depth, chef relationships, local density, and differentiated sourcing.

Ethnic restaurant suppliers may control hard-to-substitute SKUs, language/cultural selling channels, regional density, and fragmented customer relationships. This is a low-attention node but carries micro-cap, governance, liquidity, and execution risk.

Cash-and-carry gives independent operators immediacy, price discovery, and an alternative to scheduled broadline delivery. Consolidation in this channel can reduce procurement flexibility for independents.
Restaurant supply chains require frequent, temperature-sensitive, multi-SKU deliveries. Route density can lower delivery cost per case, improve service reliability, and create local scale barriers.
Perishable ingredients, proteins, dairy, frozen foods, and beverages require reliable cold-chain capacity. Failures directly affect food safety, waste, menu availability, and margin.

Proteins, dairy, grains, oils, produce, and coffee can swing restaurant gross margins. Commodity volatility is a margin catalyst but less proprietary unless a supplier controls differentiated sourcing or processing capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: B2B coffee, beverage, tea, extract, and private-label supply
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Coffee and beverage programs are high-visibility menu profit pools. Bottleneck value may sit in integrated sourcing, roasting, extraction, private-label formulation, traceability, and customer-specific beverage solutions.

Franchisors and large chains can improve franchisee economics through purchasing scale, standardized ingredients, national distribution partnerships, quality control, and advertising/data systems. This can separate durable chains from weak restaurant concepts.

supply_chain_map.node: Restaurant labor availability and service capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Driver shortages, kitchen labor, wage inflation, scheduling complexity, and service-time degradation can constrain sales even when consumer demand exists.

supply_chain_map.node: Restaurant POS, loyalty, ordering, and analytics software
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Ordering rails, loyalty programs, menu analytics, labor scheduling, and delivery integrations can improve throughput, retention, pricing, and franchise data visibility. Bottleneck value may hide in niche tools rather than restaurant brands.
Off-premise demand changes packaging, labor, commission, kitchen workflow, and price-comparison dynamics. Delivery can expand demand but also pressure margins and expose value weaknesses.

Off-premise dining and local packaging rules create demand for reliable, compliant, cost-effective packaging. Potential bottlenecks include regulatory compliance, supplier qualification, and material availability.

supply_chain_map.node: Sanitation, HI&I chemicals, pest control, and cleaning inputs
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurants need compliant sanitation, cleaning, pest control, and food-contact safety processes. This is a low-attention second-order node where suppliers, distributors, and formulation/regulatory support may be under-mapped.

supply_chain_map.node: Food-safety audits, QA, certifications, and traceability
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Chains, distributors, and franchise systems rely on food-safety protocols, supplier audits, quality assurance, traceability, and recalls management. Certification gates can create sticky vendor relationships.

supply_chain_map.node: Restaurant equipment, refrigeration, and drive-thru infrastructure
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Kitchen equipment, refrigeration, beverage equipment, drive-thru infrastructure, and maintenance determine throughput and uptime. This node may benefit from store growth, remodels, and high-throughput formats.

supply_chain_map.node: Real estate, permitting, and store buildout
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: New restaurant unit growth depends on suitable sites, permitting, construction costs, utility access, and local labor. For high-growth concepts, store-opening execution can become the limiting factor.

supply_chain_map.node: Franchise capital, royalties, and advertising funds
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Asset-light franchisors shift operating risk to franchisees while retaining royalties, brand control, and system data. Franchisee economics are therefore a key hidden constraint behind restaurant brand growth.
